This paper considers the task of performing causal mediation analysis in the federated setting where data are stored across multiple machines due to either storage limitations or privacy concerns. To the best of mine and all reviewers' knowledge, this problem setup is interesting, important, and quite novel, with no previous paper considering it. One reviewer described it as "highly understudied yet critical".

The paper builds proposes distributed versions of two classic mediation tests and proves that the proposed distributed variants achieve the same power as the non-distributed versions asymptotically, and are moreover highly communication efficient, requiring only a single round of communication. The reviewers all agreed that the proposed tests were "simple and practical" and "principled" and that the work as a whole showed "strong novelty".

In addition to synthetic studies that corroborate the theoretical results, the paper also includes an interesting case study on real-world education data, asking whether the effect of high school mathematics education on performance in college-level statistics courses is mediated by knowledge of calculus. Although the reviewers did not say much about this case study, I think it really strengthens the paper and illustrates the method's applicability.

The reviewers posed several possible weaknesses, including possibly unjustified assumptions and relation to previous work that was underdiscussed. However, the authors offered highly detailed responses which resolved these concerns in all cases.

I think this is a clear accept. I am recommending for a poster (rather than spotlight/oral) for the sole reason that the setting, while novel, seems quite niche. That said, by average score it's among the higher ones in my batch, so I would not at all be opposed to bumping it up.

We thank all reviewers for providing thoughtful and constructive feedback. In response, we have carefully considered each of the points raised and made significant revisions to the manuscript to address the concerns. Specifically, we have made the following changes in the revision, as suggested by the reviewers:

1. We have provided a detailed discussion of how our method relates to classical meta-analysis methods (Lee et al., 2015; Saunders et al., 2023), federated causal inference (Guo et al., 2024; Khellaf et al., 2024), and distributed statistical testing (Battey et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2019). We also included a comparison with the simple averaging method in the simulations, as suggested by reviewer pTFS and rUFx.

2. We discussed how our method performs in the presence of heterogeneity across machines. Additionally, we have included an extra simulation in the revised manuscript to explore the scenario of heterogeneity, as suggested by reviewers pTFS and XAfo.

3. We provided a detailed explanation of how our method handles multidimensional mediators and how it is improved according to the HDMT method proposed by Dai et al. (2022) and the JT-comp method from Huang (2019), as suggested by reviewers XAfo, aebb, and rUFx.

4. We provided an in-depth discussion of the condition $K = o(\sqrt{N})$, and also increased the value of $K$ in the simulations to examine the performance of our method when the condition is not met, as suggested by reviewers XAfo and aebb.

Through these revisions, we have found that, in addition to the advantages mentioned in the original manuscript, our method demonstrates strong performance in handling heterogeneity across centers and is robust to larger values of $K$.
 We are confident that these changes enhance the manuscript and provide clearer insights into the contributions of our work.

We sincerely appreciate the opportunity to revise our paper and believe that the revised version better reflects the significance and rigor of our research.
Thank you again for your time and effort in reviewing our submission. We look forward to your final decision.

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and thoughtful comments. We address the reviewer's questions in the following. We hope the responses below address the reviewer's concerns.

**Weakness 1:** The underlying split-and-conquer framework is not new. Prior work (e.g., Battey et al.,2018, Zhao et al., 2019) has extensively studied distributed statistical testing, and this paper appears to be a direct extension of existing methods to mediation models.

**Answer:** Thank you for your insightful comment. We would like to clarify that this paper is not a direct extension of existing methods. 

First, the hypothesis testing problems addressed in the referenced papers are different from our approach. 
Battey et al. (2018) focus on testing whether a specific coefficient $\beta_v$ in a high-dimensional generalized linear model is equal to a given value, such as testing $H_0: \beta_v = 0$. Zhao et al. (2019) test whether the regression function $E(y|X)$ equals a given parametric model, i.e., $H_0: E(y|X=x) = g(x; \theta_0)$ for some $\theta_0 \in \Theta$. In contrast, our paper addresses the testing of the product of two coefficients in a structural equation model, i.e., testing $H_0: \beta \gamma = 0$. 
For different testing problems, one must construct specific test statistics and carefully examine their statistical properties to derive rejection regions and power functions.

Additionally, Battey et al. (2018) and Zhao et al. (2019) construct distributed test statistics by taking a weighted average of local test statistics, a commonly used method, but not necessarily the optimal one. In contrast, our study develops distributed Sobel and MaxP test statistics without relying on simple weighted averaging. In our revised simulations, we added comparisons with the weighted average method and found that our approach significantly outperforms it. When $N$ is fixed, the power of the weighted average method decreases sharply as $K$ increases, while our method remains almost unaffected, achieving power nearly equivalent to that of the global method. This demonstrates the innovative nature of our approach.

We hope this clarifies the novelty of our method. We will update the manuscript to highlight these distinctions more clearly.

**Weakness 2:** The authors claim that their method can be adapted to other enhanced mediation tests (e.g., those based on Sobel’s or MaxP tests), but they do not provide concrete examples or theoretical justifications.

**Answer:** Thank you for your thoughtful comment. Indeed, there are several improvements that can be made to our method, such as the HDMT method proposed by Dai et al. (2022) and the JT-comp method from Huang (2019), both of which are well-suited for high-dimensional mediators.
Suppose there are $J$ candidate mediator variables $M_1, \dots, M_j$, leading to $J$ hypothesis tests $H_{0j}: \beta_j\gamma_j=0$. Let $T_{\beta,j}$ and $T_{\gamma,j}$ represent the test statistics for the $j$-th test. 

Huang (2019) constructs a p-value as follows:

$$
\widehat{p_{comp,j}} = F\left( \frac{T_{\gamma,j}T_{\beta,j}}{\text{Var}(T_{\gamma})} \right) + F\left( \frac{T_{\gamma,j}T_{\beta,j}}{\text{Var}(T_{\beta})} \right) - F\left( \frac{T_{\gamma,j}T_{\beta,j}}{\text{Var}(T_{\gamma}) + \text{Var}(T_{\beta})} \right),
$$

where $F(z) = 2 \int_{|z|}^{\infty} \frac{K_0(z)}{\pi} \, dz$, and $K_0(z)$ is the Bessel function with order $0$. The sample variances of $T_{\gamma,j}$ and $T_{\beta,j}$ across all tests are used to estimate $\text{Var}(T_{\gamma})$ and $\text{Var}(T_{\beta})$.

In the distributed framework, we can replace $T_{\gamma,j}$ and $T_{\beta,j}$ with the averages $\overline{T_{\gamma,j}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{\dfrac{n_k}{N}}T_{\gamma,j}^{(k)}$ and $\overline{T_{\beta,j}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_k}{N}} T_{\beta,j}^{(k)}$,  respectively. This is precisely the formula in equation (4) of the article.

Additionally, Dai et al. (2022) propose the HDMT method, which constructs the test statistic:

$$
T_{HDMT,j} = (\widehat{\pi_{01}} + \widehat{\pi_{10}}) T_{MaxP,j} + \widehat{\pi_{00}} T_{MaxP,j}^2,
$$

where $\widehat{\pi_{01}}$, $\widehat{\pi_{10}}$, and $\widehat{\pi_{00}}$ are the estimated proportions of $(\beta_j = 0, \gamma_j \neq 0)$, $(\beta_j \neq 0, \gamma_j = 0)$, and $(\beta_j = 0, \gamma_j = 0)$ across all $J$ tests, respectively. These proportions can be estimated using non-parametric methods (e.g., Storey, 2002). 

In the distributed framework, $T_{MaxP,j}$ can be replaced by the distributed test statistic $T_{MaxP,j}^{Dis}$, and $\widehat{\pi_{index}} $ can be approximated by the simple average $\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{\pi_{index}}^{(k)}$, for $index=00,01,10$.

The performance and statistical properties of the distributed test statistics constructed in this way require further study, which will be addressed in future work.

**Weakness 3:** The paper focuses exclusively on one-dimensional exposure (A) and mediator (M) variables, limiting its applicability to modern high-dimensional settings (e.g., genomics, where multiple mediators may exist). 

**Answer:**  Thank you for your insightful comment. In genomic settings, where multiple candidate mediators $M_j, j=1,\ldots,J$ may exist, a common approach is to test each mediator $M_i$ individually in the model to check for mediation effects, then move to the next mediator $M_{i+1}$ and continue the testing process until all mediators have been evaluated. By controlling the false discovery rate (FDR), one can identify which mediators exhibit significant mediation effects. An example of this approach can be found in Liu et al. (2022), in the Normative Aging Genome-Wide Epigenetic Study. Clearly, this represents a multiple hypothesis testing problem, and our method can be directly extended to handle such scenarios. Furthermore, we can improve the power of our approach by incorporating methods like DACT from Dai et al. (2022) and JT-comp method from Huang (2019), as detailed in the response to Weakness 2.

However, there is also another situation where multiple mediators $M_j, j=1,\ldots,J$ are included in a structural equation model (SEM), and interactions may exist among these mediators. In this case, the structural equations are given by:

$$
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_A A + \boldsymbol{\beta}^T M + \boldsymbol{\beta_X}^T \mathbf{X} + \epsilon_Y,
$$
$$
M_j = \gamma_{0j} + \gamma_j A + \boldsymbol{\gamma_{Xj}}^T \mathbf{X} + \epsilon_{Mj}, \quad j=1,\ldots,J.
$$

In this setting, one would need to test the hypothesis $H_0: \boldsymbol{\gamma}^T \boldsymbol{\beta} = 0$, where $\boldsymbol{\gamma}^T = (\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_J)^T$. This scenario is more complex because, even when $\boldsymbol{\gamma} \neq 0$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta} \neq 0$, their inner product may still be zero. Moreover, the distribution of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}^T \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is challenging to compute (Preacher et al., 2008). This falls outside the scope of the current paper, but it is an interesting direction for future research. We have included this discussion in the final section of the revised manuscript.


**Questions 1-3** have been already addressed  in the response to Weakness 1-3.

**Question 4:** Please add comparisons with naive distributed implementations (e.g., averaging p-values) in simulation studies to emphasize the advantage of the proposed methods.

**Answer:** We truly appreciate your recommendation to compare our approach with naive distributed implementations in the simulation studies. In the revised version of our study, we included comparisons with two weighted averaging methods:

$$T_{Sobel}^{ave} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{\frac{n_k}{N}} T_{Sobel}^{(k)},$$
$$T_{MaxP}^{ave} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{\frac{n_k}{N}} T_{MaxP}^{(k)}.$$

We found that both of these naive methods showed much poorer performance compared to our proposed method. For a fixed $N$, as the value of $K$ increased, the power of both averaging methods noticeably declined. In fact, their performance only slightly surpassed the results obtained from using the $T_{Sobel}^{(1)}$ and $T_{MaxP}^{(1)}$ statistics from just the first machine. When $K = 8$, the power of the averaging methods dropped to below 0.1, while the power of our proposed method remained identical to the global test.

These results further emphasize the robustness and efficiency of our method, showcasing how it maintains strong performance even as $K$ increases. We hope that this comparison adds more clarity and context to the advantages of our approach.

**Reference**

[1] Battey H, Fan J, Liu H, et al. Distributed testing and estimation under sparse high dimensional models[J]. Annals of statistics, 2018, 46(3): 1352.

[2] Dai J Y, Stanford J L, LeBlanc M. A multiple-testing procedure for high-dimensional mediation hypotheses[J]. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2022, 117(537): 198-213.

[3] Huang Y T. Genome-wide analyses of sparse mediation effects under composite null hypotheses[J]. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 2019, 13(1): 60-84.

[4] Liu Z, Shen J, Barfield R, et al. Large-scale hypothesis testing for causal mediation effects with applications in genome-wide epigenetic studies[J]. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2022, 117(537): 67-81.

[5] Preacher K J, Hayes A F. Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models[J]. Behavior research methods, 2008, 40(3): 879-891.

[6] Storey J D. A direct approach to false discovery rates[J]. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 2002, 64(3): 479-498.

[7] Zhao Y, Zou C, Wang Z. A scalable nonparametric specification testing for massive data[J]. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference, 2019, 200: 161-175.

We thank the reviewer again for the helpful comments and suggestions for our work. We are more than happy to address any further questions that you may have.

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and thoughtful comments. We address the reviewer's questions in the following. We hope the responses below address the reviewer's concerns.

**Weakness 1:** The asymptotic restriction of  $K$ seems strong ($K=o(\sqrt{N})$). This restricts that on average, each site cannot have a high number of samples. Such a restriction may make the results less applicable.

**Answer:** Thank you for your insightful comment.
The condition $K = o(\sqrt{N})$ is not as restrictive as it may seem at first glance. It is equivalent to $K / n_k \to 0$ as $n_k \to \infty$, meaning the number of sites $K$ is much smaller compared to the sample size within each site. This setup is quite common in practice, especially in meta-analysis, where researchers often aggregate conclusions from dozens of studies, each with hundreds or even thousands of data points. 

Furthermore, the condition $K = o(\sqrt{N})$ is widely used in distributed statistical inference and federated learning.
 In distributed frameworks, common estimation methods are categorized as either one-shot or multi-shot methods. The one-shot method specifically requires this assumption to ensure that the cumulative bias across machines can be neglected. Without this assumption, it would be challenging to guarantee the consistency of the estimates.

We acknowledge the concern regarding the applicability of this assumption and will consider how to relax or generalize it in future work.

**Weakness 2:** The scope is a bit narrow: It only considers single continuous mediator. Although this paper is the first work of this topic so this is not a severe problem.

**Answer:** Thank you for your thoughtful comment.
Regarding the consideration of multiple continuous mediators, we have addressed this issue in the final section of the revised manuscript. **Weakness 1:** The primary concern with the proposed method is the assumption of homogeneity among distributed sites. In Section 3, Equation 4, there is an implicit assumption that beta and gamma causal effects are homogeneous across all K data clusters. The manuscript should either address or comment on this assumption, since this "average" assumption is critical and should be considered case-by-case.

**Answer:** Thank you for your thoughtful question. You've raised an important point regarding the assumption of homogeneity in our method. In the manuscript, we initially assume that the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ effects are homogeneous across all data clusters. However, as highlighted by your comment, this assumption is indeed critical and may not always hold in practice.

To address this concern, we have included an additional simulation in the revised manuscript. This simulation explores a scenario where the distribution of $X$ varies across different centers, and where the parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ differ for each machine, while ensuring that the signs of $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are consistent across all centers.

In particular, we define $X^{(k)} \sim N(\mu_k 1_p, \Sigma_X)$, where $\mu_1, ..., \mu_K \sim_{i.i.d} U(-3, 3)$, and $1_p = (1, ..., 1)^T$ is a $p$-dimensional vector. The true parameter values for machine $k$ are given by:

$$\beta_k = 0.05 + e_{\beta,1}^{(k)}, 0.1 + e_{\beta,2}^{(k)}, 0.2 + e_{\beta,3}^{(k)}$$
$$\gamma_k = 0.05 + e_{\gamma,1}^{(k)}, 0.1 + e_{\gamma,2}^{(k)}, 0.2 + e_{\gamma,3}^{(k)}$$

where $e_{\beta,1}^{(k)}, e_{\gamma,1}^{(k)} \sim_{i.i.d} U(-0.02, 0.02)$, $e_{\beta,2}^{(k)}, e_{\gamma,2}^{(k)} \sim_{i.i.d} U(-0.04, 0.04)$, and $e_{\beta,3}^{(k)}, e_{\gamma,3}^{(k)} \sim_{i.i.d} U(-0.08, 0.08)$.

The results from this simulation are consistent with those obtained under the homogeneous case (as shown in Figure 4 of the manuscript). Specifically, our method performs similarly to the global test, with noticeable differences only when $K$ is particularly large ($K = 64$). This suggests that our method is well-suited to handle heterogeneity across centers.
We acknowledge that more rigorous theoretical results are needed to fully address heterogeneity, and we plan to explore this further in future research.

Once again, we appreciate your insightful feedback and hope that the additional simulation clarifies this concern. Thank you for helping us improve the manuscript.

**Weakness 2:** Another weakness of the method is the underlying Sobel and MaxP tests themselves, as highlighted in Section 2. The paper's impact could be enhanced by considering additional baseline tests.

**Answer:**  Thank you for your feedback. The Sobel and MaxP tests are indeed classical methods, and there are several improvements based on them. In the revision, we discuss the implementation of two such improvements within a distributed framework: the HDMT method proposed by Dai et al. (2022) and the JT-comp method from Huang (2019). Both of these methods are well-suited for high-dimensional mediators.

Let there be $J$ candidate mediator variables $M_1, \dots, M_j$, leading to $J$ hypothesis tests $H_{0j}: \beta_j \gamma_j = 0$. Denote $T_{\beta,j}$ and $T_{\gamma,j}$ as the test statistics for the $j$-th test.

Huang (2019) constructs a p-value as follows:

$$
\widehat{p_{comp,j}} = F\left( \frac{T_{\gamma,j} T_{\beta,j}}{\text{Var}(T_{\gamma})} \right) + F\left( \frac{T_{\gamma,j} T_{\beta,j}}{\text{Var}(T_{\beta})} \right) - F\left( \frac{T_{\gamma,j} T_{\beta,j}}{\text{Var}(T_{\gamma}) + \text{Var}(T_{\beta})} \right),
$$

where $F(z) = 2 \int_{|z|}^{\infty} \frac{K_0(z)}{\pi} \, dz$, and $K_0(z)$ is the Bessel function of order $0$. The sample variances of $T_{\gamma,j}$ and $T_{\beta,j}$ across all tests are used to estimate $\text{Var}(T_{\gamma})$ and $\text{Var}(T_{\beta})$.

In the distributed framework, we replace $T_{\gamma,j}$ and $T_{\beta,j}$ with the averages $\overline{T_{\gamma,j}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{\dfrac{n_k}{N}} T_{\gamma,j}^{(k)}$ and $\overline{T_{\beta,j}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_k}{N}} T_{\beta,j}^{(k)}$, respectively, as described in equation (4) of the paper.

Additionally, Dai et al. (2022) propose the HDMT method, which constructs the test statistic:

$$
T_{HDMT,j} = (\widehat{\pi_{01}} + \widehat{\pi_{10}}) T_{MaxP,j} + \widehat{\pi_{00}} T_{MaxP,j}^2,
$$

where $\widehat{\pi_{01}}$, $\widehat{\pi_{10}}$, and $\widehat{\pi_{00}}$ are the estimated proportions of $(\beta_j = 0, \gamma_j \neq 0)$, $(\beta_j \neq 0, \gamma_j = 0)$, and $(\beta_j = 0, \gamma_j = 0)$ across all $J$ tests, respectively. These proportions can be estimated using non-parametric methods (e.g., Storey, 2002).

In the distributed framework, $T_{MaxP,j}$ is replaced by the distributed test statistic $T_{MaxP,j}^{Dis}$, and $\widehat{\pi_{index}}$ is approximated by the simple average $\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{\pi_{index}}^{(k)}$, $index=00,01,10.$

The performance and statistical properties of these distributed test statistics will be further studied, and we plan to address these aspects in future work.

**Weakness 1:** The authors don't discuss how this relates to classical meta analysis methods that similarly aim to combine results from multiple sites.

**Answer:** Thank you very much for your insightful comment. The proposed method can be viewed as a form of meta-analysis. In the context of mediation analysis research, meta-analysis is often employed to combine results from multiple studies. This is typically done by either computing a weighted average of p-values or test statistics (Saunders et. al., 2023), or by averaging the estimated mediation effects ($\widehat{ME_k}$, for $k = 1, \dots, K$) using a weighted approach (Lee et. al., 2015), such as:

$$
\widehat{ME_{Dis}} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\widehat{ME_k}}{\hat{\sigma_k}}} {\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{1}{\hat{\sigma_k}}}.
$$

Subsequently, a confidence interval for $\widehat{ME}_{Dis}$ is computed for statistical inference. However, it is important to note that these methods often lack a detailed and rigorous statistical framework to support their use. For example, these approaches require that $K = o(\sqrt{N})$, yet this assumption is rarely discussed in the literature.

In contrast, the method proposed in this paper is grounded in a more rigorous statistical theory, offering a clear advantage in terms of precision and reliability. In the simulation of the revision, we included comparisons with two weighted averaging methods:
$$T_{Sobel}^{ave} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{\frac{n_k}{N}} T_{Sobel}^{(k)},$$
$$T_{MaxP}^{ave} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sqrt{\frac{n_k}{N}} T_{MaxP}^{(k)}.$$
We found that both of these naive methods showed much poorer performance compared to our proposed method. For a fixed $N$, as the value of $K$ increased, the power of both averaging methods noticeably declined. In fact, their performance only slightly surpassed the results obtained from using the $T_{Sobel}^{(1)}$ and $T_{MaxP}^{(1)}$ statistics from just the first machine. When $K = 8$, the power of the averaging methods dropped to below 0.1, while the power of our proposed method remained identical to the global test.

We hope this provides a clearer understanding of the value and novelty of our approach.

**Weakness 2:** The authors also don't discuss existing work on federated causal inference ([Guo et al. 24], [Khellaf et al. 24], and related works) and how their method methodologically relates.

**Answer:** Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We appreciate your reference to existing work on federated causal inference.While the mediation effect is indeed an indirect causal effect, there is a methodological distinction between causal inference and mediation analysis. In causal inference, the focus is primarily on estimating treatment effects, particularly total effects, within the potential outcomes framework. On the other hand, mediation analysis focuses more on hypothesis testing within the structural equation model framework, where the primary concern is testing for mediation effects, such as $\beta\gamma = 0$.

However, there are commonalities between causal inference and mediation analysis in terms of constructing statistics—both methodologies aim to derive meaningful statistics, with causal inference concentrating on effect estimation and mediation analysis focused on hypothesis testing. 

In the distributed framework, methods for constructing statistics generally fall into two categories: one-shot and multi-shot approaches. To estimate the Average Treatment Effect (ATE), $\tau(e)$, where $e$ is the nuisance propensity model, the simplest approach is to take the weighted average of estimates from each site, $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \eta_k \hat{\tau_k}(\hat{e_k})$. An improvement proposed by Guo et al. (2024) is to use the weighted average of the propensity estimates, $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat{\tau_k}(\sum_{r=1}^{K} \eta_r \hat{e_r})$. Khellaf et al. (2024) also studied one-shot and multi-shot methods in the context of linear outcome models. We have added the discussion in Introduction in revision.

To construct the Sobel test statistic $T_{Sobel} = T_{Sobel}(T_{\gamma}, T_{\beta})$ in the distributed setting, the simplest method is the weighted average of each site’s estimates: $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \xi_k T_{Sobel}^{(k)}(T_{\gamma}^{(k)}, T_{\beta}^{(k)})$. 
We propose an improved approach $T_{Sobel}(\bar{T_\gamma}, \bar{T_\beta})$,
where $ \bar{T_\gamma} $ and $ \bar{T_\beta} $ are the weighted averages of $ \bar{T_\gamma}^{(k)} $ and $ \bar{T_\beta}^{(k)} $ across all sites $ k = 1, \dots, K $. This method performs significantly better than the simple averaging approach.

summary.value: The manuscript proposes a framework for mediation analysis when data is stored across multiple locations and cannot be pooled together due to various reasons. The proposed solution is distributed and communication-efficient. The core idea is to use distributed versions of the classic Sobel's and MaxP tests by having each local machine compute t-test statistics and sending only these two scalars to a central server for an average aggregation. The manuscript shows that the proposed tests achieve asymptotic power nearly identical to that of a global test performed on pooled data. The paper also presents promising results from simulations and a real-data educational study, where the distributed approach successfully identifies a mediation effect not initially found in local analyses.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**

* Theoretical foundation for an unaddressed application area. The manuscript is one of the first to formalize a solution for conducting mediation analysis in a distributed data environment. Specifically, Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 are relevant as they provide a principled approach for aggregating siloed statistics into a global test under conditions over N (the amount of data) and K (the number of distributed machines). The asymptotic nature of the result in Theorem 3.2 allows the proposed method to be communication-efficient (as only two statistics are needed).
* Simple and practical. The proposed method is theoretically simple to follow, and its implementation is straightforward. This accessibility has added practical value for adoption.

**Weaknesses**

* The primary concern with the proposed method is the assumption of homogeneity among distributed sites. In Section 3, Equation 4, there is an implicit assumption that beta and gamma causal effects are homogeneous across all K data clusters. The manuscript should either address or comment on this assumption, since this "average" assumption is critical and should be considered case-by-case.
* Another weakness of the method is the underlying Sobel and MaxP tests themselves, as highlighted in Section 2. The paper's impact could be enhanced by considering additional baseline tests.

questions.value:
1. Regarding the "average" effect (see weaknesses section), how would the proposed method perform in cases where parameters beta and gamma are considerably different among K clusters? Are there any thoughts on how to adapt the framework for these cases, or a method for testing heterogeneity that would enable one to decide whether to apply the framework or not?
2. As noted in Section 4.1, when the condition K = o(sqrt(N)) is not satisfied, the power of the method is slightly lowered. Could the authors elaborate on this practical boundary? Is it possible to estimate the rate of power degradation?

My suggestion is to accept the work after reading the peer reviews and the author's rebuttals.

summary.value: This paper studies the problem of mediation hypothesis testing in a federated setting where raw observations cannot be centrally pooled. The framework is built upon classic Sobel's and MaxP tests, and hence proposes their distributed versions. The extension is comprehensive: many enhanced tests built upon those two classic tests can be easily extended to the distributed setting. The method is simple: the server computes the distributed statistics following Equations 5 and 6, but this simple method yields a closed-form solution of both tests (Theorem 3.2).

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. This paper has strong novelty. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first distributed framework for testing mediation.
2. The framework has low communication cost: each server only needs to communicate two scalars in one round without further iterations.
3. The theoretical guarantees are sound and the limits are clearly stated (value of K).

Weaknesses:
1. The asymptotic restriction of $K$ seems strong ($K = o(\sqrt{N})$). This restricts that on average, each site cannot have a high number of samples. Such a restriction may make the results less applicable.
2. The scope is a bit narrow: It only considers single continuous mediator. Although this paper is the first work of this topic so this is not a severe problem.
3. Privacy is still a major concern in distributed settings, but this paper did not provide privacy guarantees, and information leakage was not discussed.

questions.value:
Please see points 1 and 3 in Weaknesses. In particular,
1. Does the author have any idea or predictions on how the results would be if K is larger than $o(\sqrt{N})$?
3. Was the privacy discussion omitted due to technical difficulties or was it taken care of inside the framework already?

summary.value: This paper investigates mediation analysis within a distributed framework. The authors propose two novel methods: a distributed Sobel's test and a distributed MaxP test, both developed under a split-and-conquer framework. Theoretical analyses and numerical experiments demonstrate the performance characteristics of the proposed methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### **Strengths**

1. **Novel Contribution to Distributed Mediation Analysis**  
   The paper makes a valuable contribution by addressing mediation analysis within a distributed framework, where data are stored and processed across multiple worker machines due to storage or privacy constraints. The authors propose distributed versions of Sobel’s test and the MaxP test, which are communication-efficient and easy to implement. 

2. **Clear and Well-Structured Writing**  
   The paper is well-organized, with a logical flow from problem formulation to theoretical analysis, simulations, and real-world application. The abstract and introduction clearly outline the research objectives, methodology, and contributions. The theoretical results are presented rigorously, and the numerical experiments are well-documented, making the paper easy to follow.  

### **Weaknesses**  

1. **Limited Novelty in Methodology**  
   While the paper applies distributed inference to mediation analysis, the underlying split-and-conquer framework is not new. Prior work (e.g., Battey et al. [4], Zhao et al. [35]) has extensively studied distributed statistical testing, and **this paper appears to be a direct extension of existing methods to mediation models**.  

2. **Lack of Discussion on Extensions to Other Mediation Tests**  
   The authors claim that their method can be adapted to other enhanced mediation tests (e.g., those based on Sobel’s or MaxP tests), but they **do not provide concrete examples or theoretical justifications**. 

3. **Restriction to Univariate Exposure and Mediator**  
   The paper focuses exclusively on **one-dimensional exposure (A) and mediator (M) variables**, limiting its applicability to modern high-dimensional settings (e.g., genomics, where multiple mediators may exist). The authors acknowledge this limitation in Section 6 but do not propose solutions or extensions.

questions.value:
1. How does the proposed distributed mediation testing methods differ fundamentally from existing split-and-conquer approaches for general statistical inference? Please give some discussions.
2. What specific enhanced mediation tests (beyond Sobel/MaxP) could directly benefit from this distributed framework? Please give some detailed examples or discussions.
3. What modifications would be needed to handle multivariate mediators or exposures? The authors can propose a conceptual extension to multidimensional mediators, even if theoretical analysis are deferred to future work.
4. Please add comparisons with naive distributed implementations (e.g., averaging p-values) in simulation studies to emphasize the advantage of the proposed methods.

enum.description: 6: Strong Accept: Technically flawless paper with groundbreaking impact on one or more areas of AI, with exceptionally strong evaluation, reproducibility, and resources, and no unaddressed ethical considerations.

title.value: Distributed mediation analysis with  communication efficiency

abstract.value: We study the mediation analysis under the distributed framework, where data are stored and processed across different worker machines due to storage limitations or privacy concerns. Building upon the classic Sobel's test and MaxP test, we introduce the distributed Sobel's test and distributed MaxP test, respectively. These tests are both communication-efficient and easy to implement. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments show that, compared to the global test obtained by pooling all data together, the proposed tests achieve nearly identical power, independent of the number of machines. Furthermore, based on these two distributed test statistics, many enhanced mediation tests derived from the Sobel's or MaxP tests can be easily adapted to the distributed system. We apply our method to an educational study, testing whether the effect of high school mathematics on college-level Probability and Mathematical Statistics courses is mediated by Calculus. Our method successfully detects the mediation effect, which would not be identifiable using data from only the first or second class, highlighting the advantage of our approach.
